parts: "It's hard getting my first 1,000 subscribers!" Here's how to make it 10x easier 👇

1) Choosing A Niche That Has Potential While picking a niche may seem like an obvious first step, there’s actually more strategy involved than you might realize. Your niche should balance three things: your interests, the market size (TAM), and the competition level.

❤️ Interest: You’ve probably heard this before, but it’s key to create content on topics you actually enjoy. When you like what you’re doing, you’re more likely to stick with it, especially in the early days when growth is might be slow. Plus, if you’re genuinely interested, you’ll have a better understanding of your target audience’s wants and needs.

👥 TAM (Total Addressable Market): It’s important to make sure your niche has a big enough audience to support your growth. One way to do this is by checking the top creators in your niche and seeing what kind of view counts they’re averaging. 1of10 can help you a lot with this, spotting high-performing videos. Remember, aim for niches where top creators are pulling in hundreds of thousands of views telling you there a large enough market for it.

🥊 Low Competition: Instead of heading into a highly saturated niche, think about how you can differentiate yourself. It’s tough to find a niche with no competition in 2024, but you can create a “micro-niche” by focusing on a unique angle. For example, if you're in the cooking space, instead of sharing general recipe videos, you might focus on 15-minute meals for college students or cooking with minimal ingredients for people on a budget. This helps you stand out without shrinking your audience too much.

2) Finding Viral Ideas Now that you’ve chosen your niche, it’s time to find the right content ideas that will attract your audience. A method known as “outlier ideation” is a great way to spot videos that are likely to do well.

🔁 Within Your Niche: Look at what’s already working by studying the top-performing videos from creators in your space. You can use tools like 1of10 to track competitors and spot video ideas that have performed unusually well. These are known as “outliers,” and provide clues as to what kind of content could go viral for you too.
🔀 Outside your niche: Sometimes the best ideas come from adjacent niches. For example, if your channel is about photography, look at popular content in videography or graphic design.
3) Validate Your Ideas Not every idea you come up with will be worth doing. Before you spend time creating a video, you need to make sure the idea still can still do well.

📈 Look For Recent Successes: Check if other creators have had recent success with similar content. Videos that performed well months ago might not do too well today, so make sure your idea is still relevant.

📉 Avoid Overdone Formats: If you've see the same format being used over and over again, it’s probably already been saturated. You want to instead spot ideas that still have room for growth but haven’t been done to death.

4) Perfect Your Packaging (Titles and Thumbnails) Packaging is everything when it comes to getting people to click on your video on YouTube. Even the best video won’t perform well if the title and thumbnail aren’t attractive. These two elements work together to make a first impression, so you’ll need to spend time perfecting them.

📟 Thumbnails: Your thumbnail should instantly grab attention and tell a viewer what your video is about at a glance. You can compare your thumbnail against others in your niche to see how well it stands out.

✏️ Titles: Your title needs to spark some sort of curiosity or promise value while also being concise. The best titles don’t just describe the video, they make viewers feel like they need to watch it.

5) Following Niche Content Formats Before recording, study the successful creators in your niche to understand the type of content your audience likes. This includes things like video length, pacing, intros, humour, and overall style.
⏱️ Video length: Are most of the popular videos in your niche around 10 minutes, or are they shorter? Changing to the preferred length can increase your chances of holding your audience’s attention.

🛑 Pacing And Style: Some audiences prefer fast-paced content with lots of jump cuts, while others enjoy more laid-back videos. Watch how the top creators in your niche handle these elements and think about how you can adding them into your own videos.

6) Creating A Feedback Loop Once you’ve started uploading content, you can’t stop there. One of the most powerful ways to improve is by creating a feedback loop with your audience and analysing your YouTube analytics.

❔ Use Polls And Questions: YouTube’s Community Tab is a great tool for interacting with your viewers. Ask them what topics they want to see, or get feedback on what they liked or didn’t like about your last video. This not only helps you make content they enjoy, but also makes your content better getting you more views and subscribers.

📊 Look At Feedback With Your Stats: Combine what your audience says with what the numbers show. For example, if viewers are saying they loved a certain video, but your analytics show a high drop-off point, you might need to adjust the pacing or structure of future videos.
🚦 A/B Test Thumbnails: YouTube introduced A/B testing for thumbnails, giving you the ability to experiment with different designs to see which one boosts your click-through rate (CTR).

parts: How Ruhi Çenet Averages 23 Million Views Per Long Form Video Ruhi Çenet’s channel is probably one of the most interesting case studies on YouTube. With his 12 most recent longform videos, he has amassed and INSANE 275,000,000 Views. Yet, he is rarely spoken about online. In this thread, we’re going to break down exactly how he’s able to go so viral. Bookmark this to save to value 🔖 (Thread🧵)
To answer this question, let’s use this 39 Million view video as an example. Here's how he was able to go so viral👇

Let's analyze the thumbnail first: 1) Trust / Believability Viewers expect to receive PRECISELY what they were promised when they clicked. You need to have a thumbnail that supports the title. Ruhi Çenet does this perfectly in the thumbnail.

2) Colour Contrast The warm skin tones/clothes contrast with the cooler background - helping him and the town to stand out. This also helps bring attention to the gas mask which contrasts with the skin. However, contrast doesn't just relate to colours. But also to detail. The simple detail of the clouds and the sky directly contrasts with the more detailed town and person. Contrast guides the viewer's focus to certain elements in the thumbnail. Which further drives the viewer's focus on these elements.

3) Negative Association Negative emotions are attention-grabbing. The gas mask creates a sense of risk as it's associated with someone being in pain or close to death. It also depicts to the viewer that there's a lack of air (helps since the second half of the title is likely to be cut off). This sparks curiosity in viewers, forcing them to click.

4) Exaggeration / Scene Setting This can be used to emphasise certain elements within a thumbnail. Including clouds and the Earth curving in the background helps to emphasize the height of the town as being in "space".

5) Facial Expression His negative facial expression hints to the viewer that he is going to run out of air or about to pass out. This intrigues the viewer to find out what led to this and if it got worse, increasing the chances of sparking more viewers' curiosity... Therefore, increasing the possibility of them clicking.

6) Simplicity You need as little visual noise as possible. This doesn't just convey the premise of the video better... But also reduces the processing time necessary and reduces the risk of confusion for viewers - resulting in viewers scrolling. There are only 3 elements: Text Person Background

While the thumbnail is used to grab the viewer's visual attention, the title works alongside it to provide the necessary context. A great title clarifies the premise of the video and strengthens the viewer’s interest. Here's why it works:

1) Title Format The title follows a "[ACTION] the [ADJECTIVE][SUBJECT]" format. “Visiting The Closest Town to Space (Life With 50% Less Oxygen)” This title format is a viral format that has been proven to produce outliers time and time again. Below, I have found 8 examples using the 1of10 tool to find well-performing videos using this EXACT title format:

2) Extremity Using "space" as a reference point helps to exaggerate the height of the town to the viewer. This was done purposefully as in the intro, he uses "sky" as the reference rather than "space". The change from "sky" to "space" makes it more interesting (and extreme) to the viewer.

Even if your video has a great title and thumbnail, it would be meaningless if the IDEA of your content is not interesting. Here's how Ruhi Çenet's idea led to the video's success: 1) Data-Backed The "visiting unheard or extreme places" topic has been a popular and viral concept that's been shown to do well. I have found 8 more examples below using the 1of10 tool to find outlier videos that use this topic:

2) Remarkability The video idea is a remarkable, interesting concept that works with FOMO. Viewers will think... "How often will I see someone going to the closest town to space again?" So viewers feel forced to click.
The packaging may grab the viewer's attention... But Ruhi Çenet needs to retain this attention throughout the video. Here are 4 retention strategies you can steal from Ruhi Çenet:

1) Confirming The Click You need to satisfy the viewer's click. However, you can't only tell the viewer they've clicked on the right video... You need to show the viewer. Within the first 15 seconds, the click is confirmed - showing the town with no clouds, and breathing oxygen from a tank to show low oxygen levels.

2) Sense Of Risk / Increasing the Stakes The risk is established to the viewer in the intro - having the person shown coughing and saying "Not even a single tree can survive because of the low air pressure". He also establishes a second risk by mentioning that crimes are common, then reminds the viewer later in the video. This builds tension and sparks curiosity in the viewer to continue watching to see if anything went wrong.

3) Visual Explanation Visually explaining to the viewer helps them to grasp complex concepts more easily, reducing the likelihood of clicking off from feeling excluded. Here are some examples from within the video:

4) Avoiding Repetitiveness Repetition will cause boredom in a viewer. Regularly changing camera angles helps the video to feel less repetitive, especially in periods of long explanation/dialogue. Some examples are: Medium Shots Zoomed In Close Ups Overhead Shot

Finally, arguably the biggest contributor to his insane success is the fact that he does all of this, while also dubbing his content into more than 12 languages. This massively increases the TAM (Total Addressable Market) for his content, meaning that when a video of his performs well, it has a much larger audience that the content can be shown to.

parts: "I don't understand my analytics!" Let's cover the only 5 metrics you need 👇

Impressions Impressions are how many times YouTube shows your video to people. It’s pretty much the number of chances your video has to be clicked. More impressions mean more opportunities to get viewers, and that’s where it all starts. Here's how to get more impressions 👇

👥 Attract a Wider Audience: To get more impressions, your videos need to interest more than just your core subscribers. You want to make content that appeals to three groups: your core, casual viewers, and a broader audience. If your video is too niche, it might not get shown to as many people, limiting your impressions.

⚖️ Balance Niche and Broad Topics: Niche topics are great for building close and loyal subscribers, but sometimes you need broader topics to reach more people. Try making videos that balance niche content with something trending or broadly interesting. This can bring in both your core audience and new viewers.

Click-Through Rate (CTR) Of course, once YouTube starts showing your videos, you need people to click on them. CTR (Click-Through Rate) measures how good your title and thumbnail are at grabbing attention and getting viewers to click on your video. Here's how to improve CTR 👇

💡 Choose Good Video Ideas: The topic of your video matters. If it’s not interesting or relevant, people won’t click. Focus on topics your audience cares about or ones that are trending. When viewers see a topic that solves a problem or answers a question they have, they’re way more likely to click.
📝 Craft Catchy Titles: A good title should be clear and get straight to the point. It helps if you use keywords people might search for, but don’t make the title too long or confusing.

👀 Use Eye-Catching Thumbnails: Your thumbnail is the first thing people see, so it has to stand out. Use bright, high-quality images that show emotion or action. Adding a bit of text to the thumbnail (different from your title) can also help get attention.

Views Views are the number of people who actually clicked and watched your video. When you check your video’s performance, views are one of the first things to look at because they give you an overview of how well your video did overall. Here's how to get more views 👇

💯 Look at Your Best Videos: Check out the videos on your channel that have the most views. What do they have in common? Is it the topic, the thumbnail, or maybe the editing style? Once you figure out what’s working, use those ideas in your future videos to help raise your views.

🎥 Keep Viewers Watching: Getting views is great, but keeping people watching is even better. If your videos consistently get high views, it means people are not only clicking but staying too. When people stick around for the majority of your video, YouTube tends to recommend your videos to even more people.

Average View Duration (AVD) Average View Duration (AVD) tells you how long people stay on your video. The longer people watch, the more YouTube pushes your video. That’s why having a high AVD is incredibly important. Here's how to increase AVD 👇
🎣 Strong Hooks: The first few seconds of your video are vital. Make sure your intro gets straight to the point and delivers on what your title and thumbnail promised.

🎬 Keep It Short and Interesting: Don't make your video longer than it needs to be by adding extra stuff. People get bored quickly, so stick to sharing important content and keep it interesting the whole time.
📜 Storytelling: Everyone enjoys a good story. Including personal stories or examples keeps people interested and gives them a reason to watch until the end.

🛑 Effective CTAs (Call to Action): At the end of your video, tell your viewers to keep watching. Recommend other videos on your channel or ask them to subscribe or buy your product/service, but make sure it's quick and on topic.

Retention Graphs Retention graphs show you where people stopped watching or skipped ahead in your video. If you want to know what keeps people engaged and makes them leave, look at your retention graph. Here are the different types of retention graphs 👇

Early Peak: If your graph has a sharp spike early on, it might mean your intro is dragging on. Viewers are skipping ahead to where the real content starts. Keep your intro short and get to the value quickly. Gradual Decline: A steady drop-off throughout the video could mean that viewers feel like they’ve already gotten what they came for. You might need to work on pacing and making it clear why they should stick around for the rest of the video. Spikey Graphs: If your graph spikes at certain points, it means people are skipping ahead to different sections. This usually happens when you reveal your key points too early, and viewers feel they don’t need to watch and wait for you to explain.

parts: If I Were Starting a Youtube Channel in 2024, I’d Do This. Growing a YouTube channel from scratch is no easy task. However, with the strategy outlined in this thread, you’ll not only avoid the most common fatal errors, but also learn how to create videos with the best chance of going viral (Going viral is a science, not luck). P.S If you’re a complete beginner, come back to this later. First you just need to start making some videos and learn the basics! (Bookmark this so you don’t lose the value!)

Step 1: Choosing A Niche While choosing your niche may seem like a straightforward step, there's actually a strategic approach you can take to ensure you pick a niche with good potential. This ultimately comes down to 3 main factors, which can be seen below. 1. Interest. This may sound cliche, but it is important to enjoy the content you’re producing, especially at the beginning. Not only because you’ll be more likely to stick at it, but also because you’ll have a deeper understanding of your target audience, which you can leverage to your advantage. 2. TAM. You need to ensure that your niche has a large enough total addressable market. Otherwise, getting the number of views per video you want may be extremely difficult, if not impossible. More on how to check this coming up 👇 3. Low Competition. While this isn’t essential, selecting a niche or at least a sub-niche, with lower competition will make the process of going viral a lot easier. More details on how to do this below.

Validating Your Total Addressable Market Once you have chosen a niche that you enjoy, it’s now time to validate the total addressable market (TAM) to ensure that there are enough viewers to reach the goals you have in mind. A good indicator for finding the TAM is to look at what the top few creators in your niche are averaging in terms of views. The easiest way to do this is to download the free 1of10 extension (link in bio), then head over to your competitors channel and look for videos with an outlier score between 0.8x and 1.2x. This will quickly highlight the channels recent average. You can also have a look at their highest outliers for a rough idea of what the potential view ceiling could look like for some topics. You’re ideally looking for an average view count in the hundreds of thousands or higher (There are a few exceptions to this rule, though)

Creating/Finding a Low Comp Niche Finding a niche with very low competition on YouTube in 2024 is like looking for a needle in a haystack. Instead of trying to find the impossible, you’re much better off looking for a way to differentiate yourself from the competition and thus create your own micro sub-niche. There are many ways to do this, for example, you could produce higher quality content than others in your niche, you could make content in a different style / length / depth, or finally, you could niche down further (be careful not to shrink your TAM too much doing this).

Step 2: Finding Ideas Once you’ve found a high-potential niche, the next step is to find an idea to reach this new audience. We’ve found the most reliable way of finding ideas that consistently go viral is to use an outlier ideation method. This essentially consists of finding videos that over-performed (outliers), and then adapting these ideas to create new unique videos for your channel (while keeping the elements that made it go viral in the first place). When it comes to outlier ideation, there are 3 main ways you can find ideas: 1. From within your channel. 2. From within your niche. 3. From outside your niche. As this is a new channel, we’ll focus on methods 2 & 3.

Finding Ideas From Within Your Niche The best way to find outliers from within your niche is using the 1of10 app (you can also do this on YouTube, it will just take much longer). Firstly, you want to create a list of all competitors within your niche and add these channels to a tracked channel folder. Next, filter this folder to only show videos uploaded within the last 6 months, at least a 2x outlier score, and more than 100k views (you may need to tweak these settings depending on the results). Now, look for patterns in ideas & titles in order to find a good outlier format (the larger the outlier score, the better).

Analysing The Format After you’ve selected some idea formats, you next need to breakdown exactly why you think these formats/videos performed well. From here, it makes it easier to adapt the idea, while keeping the viral aspects.

Adapting The Format: Once you understand why a format performed well, you can then begin to adapt the idea to create a unique video. For example, in 1of10 we can see that there are several outlier videos in the soccer niche focused on Diego Maradona. This suggests that he himself could be a viral theme / has viral potential and would make sense to use as the subject of our video. Suggestion: The Entire History of Diego Maradona

Finding Ideas From Outside Your Niche Finding ideas from outside your niche is where things get a little more tricky. To start, you first want to create a list of adjacent niches. Sticking with the Soccer niche, these could be things like, Basketball, Hockey, NFL & Baseball. It’s important to find niches with similar audience characteristics, as this will give you the best chance of finding ideas that resonate with your audience. Once you’ve found several adjacent niches, you next want to create tracked channel folders for each of these in 1of10. Again, using the same filters we outlined earlier, browse through these folders and look for patterns in ideas and titles. Ideally, here you’ll be looking for idea formats that have worked across several different niches, as this is a great validator to suggest it could work in your niche too. Once you’ve found an idea format, follow the steps outlined earlier.

Finalising Your Ideas Once you’ve got a list of data-backed ideas, it’s time to validate these ideas and find which ones are suitable for moving forward with. To do this, you’ll want to look at how many outliers there are for each idea format, how recently the last outliers were uploaded, and whether you can find recent examples of people using this format without success on YouTube. Ideally, the idea format will not have been done countless times, it will have recent viral examples, and there won’t be any examples of creators who attempted the format without success recently (excluding examples where the reasons are obvious). Any ideas that don’t meet these criteria can be removed from your list (you may have to go back to the previous step, but it’s worth it to find a great idea).

Step 3: Packaging Your Idea Once you have decided on the idea you would like to move forward with, it’s time to create the packaging concepts. A great place to start with this is by looking at the outlier videos that inspired this idea and try to dissect the reasons for why that packaging worked so well. Once you know the reasons why it worked, creating your own packaging becomes much easier. To help with this, you can pull the video up in 1of10, and then select ‘See Similar Thumbnails’ (See example below).

You can then filter these results and use this for inspiration for both the title and thumbnail format. It’s a good idea to prepare at least 2 thumbnails in a completely different style, as you’ll be testing these later on. (This can also be a great way for finding new idea formats)

Step 4: Following Niche Formats Now that the idea, title and thumbnail have been decided, it’s almost time to start creating your video. However, first it’s worth taking a moment to understand the type of content your audience likes to consume. To do this, watch some videos from the biggest creators in your niche, and see whether you can spot any patterns in the video length, pacing, intro style, humour etc. After this, it’s time to make the video!

Step 5: Final Checks Once you’ve finished creating the content, it’s a good idea to check your final packaging concepts to ensure that they’re clear and stand out on the home page. The best way to do this is using the free 1of10 extension. From here, you can upload your thumbnail and title to see how it would look on the YouTube homepage!

Step 6: Upload As you may know, Youtube are now rolling out the thumbnail A/B test feature to all channels. It’s a good idea to test at least 2 entirely different thumbnail concepts for each video. Once a winner has been determined, you can then refine your test further by making several variations of the winning format (ie. testing different text variants or colours in the thumbnail). You can repeat this process several times as long as the video continues to get impressions.

Step 7: Test, Iterate & Learn Finally, the most important step - refining / learning! It’s unlikely that every video you make performs well, so it’s important to reflect on videos that performed badly in order to learn from what went wrong and what you can do differently moving forward. parts: If I were starting a YouTube channel in 2025, I’d do THIS. Growing a YouTube channel is NOT easy, however if you follow the step by step process outlined in this thread you’ll be ahead of 99% of other creators starting out. You’ll learn the science of: Outlier ideation to immediately start generating views Avoiding fatal mistakes that RUIN your channel Growing faster than your competition Making more money P.S. This is a detailed insight into YouTube strategy that actually works (our team combined has over a billion views worth of YouTube strategy). Bookmark this so you don’t lose out!

Step 1. Choosing your niche. To find the “perfect” niche ask yourself these questions: 1. Do you have enough experience or interest to provide enough unique value on the topics you want to make videos on? 2. What’s the TAM (total addressable market) of the niche you have chosen? We know these questions aren’t always easy to answer so here’s what to do if you’re lost 👇

Experience and Interest YouTube is BEYOND saturated with so many creators across different niches it’s incredibly hard to stand out if you don’t find a unique angle. But how do you find your unique angle? Remember the YOU in YouTube (sounds cheesy I know), by framing your videos around your own personal stories and opinions that only you have. This instantly creates content that is unique to you and builds an audience that isn’t just interested in your ideas, but also become invested in you as a host.

Validating The Total Addressable Market (TAM) Without a high enough TAM, it doesn’t matter how “good” your videos are because there won’t be anyone there to watch them. To validate whether your niche or idea has a high enough TAM, you can search keywords relating to your niche and browse channels using the free 1of10 extension (link in bio) to observe video outlier scores. Simply click on a channel, make sure you’re on “latest” videos, and scroll to spot videos within the range of 0.8x to 1.2x. These are your “average” performing videos and give you a general idea of the TAM. On the other hand if you sort by “Descending” with the 1of10 extension, you can see what the view ceiling is for particular topics (or even idea formats). Generally you’ll want to try and grow in a niche where the TAM can supply you with at least a 100k views a video, but this might not be necessary if you’re targeting a niche audience for business purposes.

Step 2. Ideas. Ideas are what define the success of your channel and the most reliable reliable approach is “outlier ideation”. What this means is finding outlier videos (over-performing videos) to either model your content off, remix the idea or to identify “viral elements” to help your videos go viral. There are 3 approaches to outlier ideation: 1. Ideate from your own channel. 2. Ideate from within your niche. 3. Ideate from outside of your niche (and even outside of YouTube)

Ideating From Your Own Channel Ideating from your own channel is simply doubling down on what is working already. If you upload and the video ends up being an outlier, identify what it was about that video that made it an outlier and repeat it. This could be a certain subject, a particular idea format or trending topics. If identifying and remixing outlier ideas is something you find challenging, 1of10’s idea generator simply scans your channel and remixes outlier ideas for you.

Ideating from within your niche Ideating from within your niche starts with finding outlier videos from all of the channels you consider competition. This takes a long time manually browsing on YouTube, but it takes seconds to start finding outliers within 1of10’s outlier search. To start begin searching keywords relating to your niche and create a tracking folder for all of the top performing creators. After adding at least 30 channels, click on your tracking folder and filter by “score”. What this does is instantly reveal all of the top performing outliers from your niche. Study these outliers to understand why audiences enjoyed watching them, see if you can spot patterns and remix the ideas into your own content.

Remixing an Outlier Remixing an outlier can be as simple as finding a different subject to insert into an idea format. In this example you can see how many channels have remixed the “Why is sucks to be born as ..” format. The videos with the most entertaining storytelling and subjects won.

Finding Outliers From Outside Your Niche Finding great ideas from outside your niche is a little more complex, but can be extremely rewarding for your channel. To start, begin tracking channels from adjacent niches to your own. Adjacent niches are important because they can offer insights into audiences similar to your own (and therefore great potential ideas for videos). Examples of adjacent niches: Golf - Baseball - Football - Basketball (All Sports related audiences) Roblox - GTA - Minecraft (All Gaming related audiences) Painting - Sewing - Drawing (All Art related audiences) Once again, using 1of10 to create tracking folders filled with channels from your adjacent niches makes outlier ideation quick and easy. An indicator of a great idea format is one that is working across several niches. If you’re the first creator to test an outlier idea format in your niche, the potential for views increases significantly.

Validating your Ideas This is the point where you need to be CAREFUL. Sometimes you might think you have a great idea with the data to support it, but in the current landscape of YouTube the format is DEAD. To confirm whether your idea has potential, search for more recent uploads under the same format (within the past 3 to 6 months) and see if creators are still having success. Some outlier formats become so popular that they become overused, outdated and audiences are no longer interested in watching after a while. If you search your idea format and find recent uploads that aren’t doing too well, take it as a sign that the “outlier” format is no longer working.

Step 3. Packaging your idea (Thumbnail + Title) Your packaging defines how many people click on your video and is the most important aspect after your idea. Browsing all of the outlier videos you’ve collected so far is a great resource to spot top tier packaging. parts: MrBeast’s blowup - From 0 to 266,000,000 Subscribers 🏆 A thread on how MrBeast became the most subscribed YouTuber on the planet 🧵

Jimmy Donaldson, aka MrBeast created his YouTube channel on the 20th of February 2012, at the age of 13. Since then, I've identified 8 key phases along MrBeasts journey that have led to him becoming the most successful YouTuber of all time.

Phase 1: Gaming The Gaming phase on MrBeasts channel saw him reach his first 10,000 views in October 2012. However, his subscriber growth was minimal, gaining just a handful of new subscribers during this time period. It wasn’t until almost 1 year later, in August 2013, where Jimmy celebrated reaching 300 subscribers.

Phase 2: Money and Social Hacking Era Here we see a huge shift in the topics of his videos transitioning from generic gameplay content, to more of a focus around famous YouTubers and money. For example, his ‘How much does PewDiePie make?’ video. It is here where the MrBeast channel first begins to see some momentum, gaining more than 300 subscribers in November 2013 alone, and later reaching 1000 subscribers in April 2014. This new growth is partly due to MrBeast’s transition away from a hyper-competitive gaming niche, but also because his new content often leveraged social hacking by using popular YouTubers in his titles and thumbnails.

Phase 3: Random As Hell During this phase, MrBeast was uploading content almost daily and covering a broad range of topics and video styles. While the MrBeast channel did not see exponential growth in the phase, it is likely that this experimental content provided Jimmy with valuable insights into what content works on Youtube and how to better game the algorithm.

Phase 4: All or Nothing In 2016, MrBeast was given an ultimatum by his mother. Either go to college or move out. While Jimmy did choose to go to college, he secretly stopped attending lectures after just 2 weeks. This meant he essentially had until the end of the semester to make YouTube work… (Video from Colin and Samir Podcast on YouTube)

It was during the ‘All or Nothing’ phase where MrBeast attempted some of his craziest videos yet, such as, counting to 100,000. This video blew up, reaching more than 6 million views at the time and helping the MrBeast channel surpass 600,000 Subscribers. This video also opened up a new bucket of extreme content for Jimmy's channel, which lead to millions more views. Other similar videos include, 'Watching It's Everyday Bro For 10 Hours Straight' & 'Saying Logan Paul 100,000 Times'

Phase 5: Giving Back On June 15, 2017, uploaded a video where he gave $10,000 to a homeless man using his brand deal money. This turned out to be a viral formula for the MrBeast channel, combining large sums of money with generosity / positivity. This video also laid the foundations for Jimmy’s 'Reinvest Everything' mindset towards making content on youtube.

During this phase, the MrBeast channel grew from around 1 million subscribers in June 2017, to a whopping 9 million subscribers in October 2018. This reinforced his belief that positivity can go as viral as negativity as long as the content is good!

Phase 6: Going Mainstream On October 26th 2018, MrBeast uploaded the ‘Ordering Water Then Tipping $30,000’ video, which later went on to get significant news coverage around the United States. Prior to this video, MrBeast was averaging 90 Million views per month, however, after this initial spike, his monthly average more than doubled to around 200 million views.

Phase 7: Post Squid Game Era The legendary MrBeast Squid Game video marked the beginning of a new era for the MrBeast channel. Not only was it his most viewed video (615 Million Views), but it also signified a drastic step-up in terms of budget, production and set quality. Very few, if any, YouTubers have been able to match this since.

Phase 8 (Current Phase): Story-Focused Until recently, MrBeast videos were relentlessly fast-paced and high energy, but over the last year, we’ve seen a noticeable slow down in the pacing of his content, in exchange for longer videos, more authenticity and better story-telling. As it stands, it looks as though this has had a positive effect on MrBeasts channel as he is currently averaging more than 2 billion views per month, which is almost double compared to 12 months ago. As for what phase is next, only time will tell!

parts: How to get monetized on YouTube with one video 👇 Getting monetized on YouTube can be hard for creators, but with the strategy outlined in this thread, we will be breaking down not only how to get monetized, but how to do it with just one video. (Bookmark this for your next video)

First, you will need to find out if your niche has a large enough total addressable market. If your niche is too small, getting the views needed to hit the watch time target and 1000 subscribers will be hard. A good way to see if you have a large enough TAM is to see what the top 20% of creators in the niche are averaging in views.

If their average views are high enough (the target should be in the hundreds of thousands), you can model 80% of their views as the potential TAM. Once you have validated the TAM, you need to find an idea to reach this new audience.
The best way to do this is to look at outliers from all of your competitors and find patterns in their ideas, titles, and thumbnails. You can easily do this by using 1of10 or the free extension.

Once you find a good outlier format, it's worth taking some extra time to validate it. This can be done by seeing when the outliers were made and how many there are. If they are older, it may be worth skipping over them as they may no longer be relevant, and if there are many similar outliers with the same format, it's likely too saturated.

Ideally, you are looking for some validation in the form of 2-3 videos that were outliers, but still have room to create your own twist and be interesting to the audience. Another way that you can do this is by still using outlier ideation and adopting style transference. Taking one style from another niche and just adding it to your own. Again, following the previous steps above, look outside the niche rather than inside.

Once you have validated the TAM and found an outlier format to create a video around, you're nearly there to getting monetized with your first video. The last thing you must do is focus on the audience and what works. This includes average video length, editing style, cuts per minute, cadence, b-roll, and everything else that makes up the actual video.

parts: I trained an AI agent to study YouTube’s open-source research... this is why the algorithm intentionally kills your video’s reach 👇
Before we get into it, I post a lot of AI X YouTube threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. reach decay is real your video isn't shadowbanned it’s just getting outdated in the algorithm’s eyes youtube uses a mechanism called temporal decay — and it's built directly into the recommendation model

2. the algorithm penalizes age every video has a kind of “freshness score” under the hood as time passes, that score fades — fast even if your video performed great on day 1, by day 30, it needs new signals to stay relevant

3. why? the training data is time-biased neural networks learn from historical data so they naturally favor videos that did well in the past but this creates a problem: 📉 it biases the model against new content 📉 and locks in old viral videos forever

4. youtube fixed this with a feature called “example age” they literally feed the age of the training example into the neural net during training: it knows the example is 7 days old during serving: it pretends the example is brand new this forces the model to stay fresh, and helps new videos go viral

5. but temporal decay still exists even with fixes, the model still weights recency older impressions get devalued stale candidates drop in rank inactive videos slowly fade from the system this is why you see views die down after the first 24–72 hours

6. reach decay varies by niche temporal decay is not fixed a viral news video decays faster than a slow-burn documentary the decay rate changes based on: - topic - user interest over time - click & watch trends per niche the algorithm adapts based on content life cycle

7. how to beat the decay there’s only one way to keep a video alive in the feed: ⚡ generate new watch time ⚡ get clicks from new users ⚡ spark new comments, shares, or embeds every new signal resets the clock just a little
8. youtube doesn’t just want good videos it wants good videos people still care about your video can be a masterpiece - but if no one’s clicking or watching it now the algorithm moves on

9. creators who win long-term do this: optimize for both burst & shelf life re-promote evergreen videos remix or follow-up on past hits build videos that compound over time (guides, lists, case studies)

when we say burst & shelf life - we refer to: Burst: Hook viewers early to win the initial algorithm boost Shelf: but build long-term value so the video keeps ranking in recommendations/search for weeks or months
10. bottom line: your video isn’t dying the algorithm is just evolving reach decays by design but attention revives it

tl;dr: YouTube’s algorithm applies temporal decay to every video Without ongoing engagement signals — clicks, watch time, retention — your content gradually loses ranking power Freshness isn’t optional Reach is a function of current relevance, not historical performance

To counter this decay, you need to inject fresh signals into the system: - Reintroduce your content to new audiences - Create follow-up or related content that loops back to it - Build videos that answer timeless questions (evergreen content)

parts: I used AI to analyze YouTube’s algorithm... and here’s why your news content might be getting "shadowbanned" 👇
Before we get into it, I post a lot of AI X YouTube threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. Researchers ran the most detailed YouTube audit ever They built over 100,000 fake users (sock puppets) - bots trained to simulate real people across 5 ideologies: - very-left - left - center - right - very-right Each bot watched 100+ politically aligned videos, then followed YouTube’s recommendations - homepage, autoplay, everything

2. Brand new accounts see mostly center & left-leaning news Researchers created fresh, clean accounts with no watch history The result? → Homepage recommendations were mostly Center or Mainstream Left → Far Right or Far Left content was nearly invisible Even without clicking anything, YouTube already nudges you Left

3. Once you train the algorithm, bias shows up - fast Trained right-leaning bots saw more ideologically consistent recommendations Trained left-leaning bots did too - but there’s a catch: 📊 It took 27 videos to shift a bot into Far Left territory ⚠️ But just 2 videos to push it out of Far Right YouTube actively resists right-leaning content... and clings longer to left-leaning patterns.

4. Fake news is NOT what’s driving this bias To test the “misinformation excuse,” the researchers ran a fake-news detection model on 11.5 million videos What they found: - Fake/misleading content was negligible - It was evenly distributed across Left and Right So the suppression isn’t about trust or truth, it's about algorithmic preference

5. Homepage recommendations are ideologically “congenial” Once bots were trained, the homepage became an echo chamber: - Right bots got mostly right content - Left bots got mostly left content - Far-right bots saw the most ideological consistency BUT: the algorithm still injected occasional cross-cutting content Left bots saw some Right videos Right bots saw almost none from the Left

6. Autoplay pushes right-leaning users deeper Researchers followed YouTube’s “up-next” trail - autoplay without user clicks - For right-leaning bots: Recommendations got more ideologically extreme as autoplay continued Exposure to “very-right” videos increased by 37% over 20 recs - For left-leaning bots: Exposure stayed flat No meaningful rise in Far Left content Autoplay = passive radicalization path… but only in one direction

7. Problematic channels do show up - but not in huge numbers Researchers used existing lists of “problematic” channels (alt-right, conspiracies, QAnon, etc.) Results: - These made up only ~2.5% of total recommendations BUT: over 36% of users encountered at least one Very-right bots saw them the most, especially deeper in the autoplay trail

8. Creators don’t need a strike to lose reach YouTube doesn’t need to ban you to bury your content The papers show 3 ways your reach can vanish: - You’re not shown on the homepage - You’re excluded from autoplay trails - New users never discover your niche No warnings - No flags Just algorithmic invisibility

9. Even mainstream news channels weren’t safe They trained bots only using Fox News or MSNBC videos Guess what? Fox-trained bots saw recommendations from alt-lite (hard right) and conspiracy channels MSNBC-trained bots mostly saw mainstream or neutral content Same starting point Different algorithmic future

10. Bottom line: YouTube isn’t banning political content - it’s nudging the narrative Its algorithm favors: - Center & Left news by default - Suppresses Far Left & Far Right - And pulls users away from right-leaning niches faster and more aggressively Your content isn’t broken The playing field is

tl;dr: YouTube isn’t outright banning political content It’s shaping what people see - subtly, consistently, and at scale → Left and Center content is algorithmically favored → Right-leaning creators face faster decay and limited discovery → The deeper you go, the more filtered your feed becomes No strikes or bank, just "silence"

If you wanna look deeper in the research papers: 1. Auditing YouTube's Recommendation System for Ideologically Extreme Content" (2022) - Authors: Magdalena Wojcieszak, et al. 2. YouTube's Recommendation Algorithm Is Left-Leaning in the United States (2023) - Authors: Manoel Horta Ribeiro, et al.

3. Your title + thumbnail = a promise your intro/hook = the confirmation if you don’t deliver the feeling of the story the viewer expected, they’ll bounce the algorithm assumes mismatch - and suppresses your content
4. A strong opening does 3 things instantly → validates the click → opens a curiosity loop → hints at a payoff worth waiting for miss one, and you're playing with a handicap

5. Bad openings come from over-explaining "what's up everyone" "today we're gonna take a look into.." "before we get into it.." → all signal to the viewer: this video isn’t urgent youtube punishes friction especially in the hook

6. Good openings compress time they skip setup and cut straight to momentum → use cold opens → show conflict early → reverse the structure (start with payoff, explain later) your first 15 seconds should feel like you're already deep into something worth finishing
7. The intro sets emotional tone humor - tension - shock - inspiration the algorithm picks up on engagement spikes and downstream behavior emotion increases watch time watch time increases reach
8. Intro → mid spike → late payoff that’s the structure the hook buys you attention the mid spike buys you completion the payoff buys you satisfaction no hook = no one sees the rest

9. Faceless or not - viewer psychology is the same it doesn’t matter if it’s a documentary or a talking head finance channel every viewer wants 3 things: → relevance → momentum → reward your intro is where all three must be promised

Example: Title “This Guy Lost $4M in a Single Bet” Bad intro (no relevance): “So before we get into that, let me tell you how gambling works...” Good intro (strong relevance): “This man walked into a casino with $10 million - and left owing the house everything.”

10. If you win the first 15 seconds, the system bets on you YouTube tests every video with small batches of traffic if retention holds, it expands if it drops, it stops your edit doesn’t matter if your hook loses the viewer before it even starts
tl;dr your title gets the click your first 15 seconds earn the algorithm's trust optimize for that moment - and the rest of your video will actually have a chance to blow up

parts: I used AI to decode how YouTube tests channels to build trust with the algorithm from day 1 Pass it, and your videos get pushed Fail it, and you get stuck at 0 A thread 🧵
Before we get into it, I post a lot of AI X YouTube threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. Youtube doesn’t trust new channels by default it doesn’t know who you are, what niche you're in, or how viewers will respond to your content so before it pushes your video - it tests you and what you do before uploading matters more than you think

2. Watch history influences recommendations - even before uploads Studies show YouTube personalizes recommendations for brand-new accounts based purely on what they watch, not just what they post → warm-up tip: watch 10–30 videos in your niche before uploading this helps the algorithm pre-classify your channel

3. Priming your account mimics real user behavior In experiments, bots that watched niche-relevant content before uploading got better-aligned recommendations → warm-up tip: if your channel is about football, binge top football creators first you’re signaling what ecosystem you belong to

4. Don’t just skim - watch with depth watching a video to 50–100% sends a much stronger signal than bouncing early → warm-up tip: let videos play through the algorithm tracks watch depth to build trust and topic familiarity

5. Verifying your account unlocks credibility bots in research had to verify to act like creators Unverified = consumer mode → warm-up tip: verify your phone number + email before uploading this shows YouTube you’re not just lurking - you’re building

6. You’re not hacking the algorithm - you’re training it YouTube builds an internal model of your channel before your first upload ever hits the homepage your job is to feed it clean, focused signals so when you post… it already knows where to send your content

7. Your first 10 uploads are your algorithmic resume they define your niche, tone, pacing, and viewer behavior if your first 10 are messy? so is the model’s understanding of your channel → treat them like a blueprint for the system to follow

8. Early upload behavior is permanently remembered research shows that initial performance shapes your channel embedding - the representation used for future recommendations → bad retention + inconsistent topics = long-term damage → good structure = compounding reach

9. Random uploads = no momentum if you switch styles, post at random times, or delete videos… you’re confusing the system → create consistency in topic, format, and pacing it builds algorithmic trust faster than spikes ever could

10. You don’t need to go viral - you need to be clear your first uploads aren’t about blowing up they’re about teaching the algorithm who you are and who you’re for → clarity > virality → session depth > view count → consistency > chaos

tl;dr YouTube doesn’t wait for your video to go live to start judging your channel it’s watching before you ever upload - warm up your account (watch, verify, finish videos) - post with clarity - build your first 10 like a portfolio train the system earn its trust then grow

parts: Two creators post nearly the same video - one goes viral, the other dies same topic, same pacing, same niche here’s why YouTube gives completely different results to similar content 👇
Before we get into it, I post a lot of YouTube related threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇
1. The algorithm doesn’t rank your video based on quality it ranks based on context - where your video lands inside YouTube’s internal content map and that “context” decides everything

2. Every video gets dropped into a giant map of youtube content the algorithm doesn’t see your video as a file - it sees it as a set of patterns: title, tone, topic, pacing, voice, structure then it places your video next to others that feel similar that placement determines who you get compared to - and what you're shown next to

3. Two similar videos can land in totally different neighborhoods how? → different titles = different click behavior → different thumbnails = different expectations → different metadata = different initial classification → different channel history = different embedding bias the result: completely different baselines

4. Your video isn’t judged in isolation - it’s judged against its neighbors you’re not competing with the global trending tab you’re competing with whatever the algorithm thinks is most similar to you → weak neighbors? you win → elite neighbors? good luck

5. Early data shifts your placement your first 1,000 impressions are like your handshake with the system if early viewers bounce? you get placed near weak or chaotic content if they stay and binge? you get upgraded to stronger clusters that’s where compounding begins

6. Packaging sends embedding signals before you upload your title, description, and even your transcript shape your coordinates → same video, slightly different framing = different position → different position = different competition → different competition = different result

7. Channel history pulls you toward certain zones your previous uploads act like magnetic anchors if you try to change niche, tone, or format too fast - you’ll get pulled back toward your old embedding that’s why pivots often flop

8. Two creators, same topic, same script - one goes viral, one dies not luck not content quality just different neighborhoods one was ranked next to bangers the other got buried next to flops same video - wrong context

9. You can train the system where to place you with consistent: → packaging → pacing → storytelling structure → topic + emotion you sharpen your channel’s coordinates - and make YouTube more confident about who to show you to

10. The algorithm isn’t random - it’s relational you don’t win by being good you win by being good in the right cluster same video, different placement = different outcome it’s not what you made - it’s where the system thinks it belongs

tl;dr YouTube doesn’t rank your video globally it ranks you next to what you resemble so two creators can make the same video - but only one gets discovered because the algorithm isn’t asking “is this good?” it’s asking: “who is this like?”

parts: I used AI to break down how the youtube algorithm treats different niches.. and here’s how to reverse-engineer exactly what the system wants from yours 👇

1. Every niche has a different algorithmic fingerprint a 12-minute storytime doesn’t get ranked the same way as a 45-minute podcast or a 3-minute animation the algorithm learns viewer expectations per niche - and ranks videos based on how well they match them

2. The algorithm doesn’t judge content in isolation your video isn’t competing with “everything on YouTube.” it’s competing with: - similar creators - similar formats - similar topics - what your viewers usually watch you're being ranked within context, not globally

3. Your job is to study the context if you want to grow in your space, you need to reverse-engineer: - the average retention in your niche - the length YouTube seems to favor - the upload frequency top channels stick to - title/thumbnail patterns that drive CTR - emotional tone that gets rewarded

4. How to start: create a mini watchlist of winners grab 10–15 videos from your niche that: - got strong velocity (views fast) - came from similar-sized or smaller channels - were published in the last 3–6 months - aren’t from mega influencers these are the real algorithm-friendly examples to learn from

5. Measure what matters (not what’s visible) don’t just copy the thumbnails look deeper: - how long was the hook before they cut? - when did they switch visuals? - what emotional tone did they open with? - where did the drop-off happen? these are retention levers - not just content ideas

6. Every niche runs on topic cycles viewers in your space follow waves of interest - and the algorithm rides them - in tech: product drops trigger discovery waves - in fitness: January, summer, and pre-holiday seasons boost traffic - in education: watch time spikes around exam periods - in sports like football: transfer windows, major tournaments, and big match days drive huge bursts of search + engagement upload the right video at the wrong time? the algorithm won’t care hit the cycle, and even average videos can explode

7. Find your niche’s “format ceiling” you can go longer or deeper - but only if viewers are trained to expect it example: → in true crime, 20–45 min is normal → in memes, 90 seconds is long → in tutorials, 6–10 min is the sweet spot break that, and your retention tanks

8. Don’t guess what works. Model it. the top creators in your niche are already training the algorithm on your behalf your job? → watch what they feed it → measure how the system rewards them → build your format around the signals that are clearly working

9. Stop copying. Start decoding. when you reverse-engineer your niche: - you don’t just upload “what you like.” - you upload what the algorithm expects - and what your viewers are already conditioned to want. good content + good alignment = exponential reach

A perfect case study for this thread is a YouTube channel called "Top Bins" Entered one of the most saturated/competitive niches and stayed on top within a year The power of being original within what already works

tl;dr YouTube doesn’t treat every niche the same It rewards content that matches what viewers in that space already engage with If you want growth, don’t just be original Be original within the framework your niche already rewards

Before we get into it, I post a lot of YouTube related threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. The market is never too crowded “everyone’s already doing that idea” “it’s impossible to grow in this niche” all wrong you’re not in a saturated market - you’re in a saturated supply here’s the difference (and how to fix it) 👇

2. On YouTube, markets don’t die - attention does your niche can stay hot, but if every video looks the same, people stop noticing the brain filters out repetition - it’s a survival feature - if it feels like something we've seen before, we scroll past, even if it’s great familiar = forgettable and forgettable doesn’t earn the click
3. That’s why copying viral ideas eventually fails even if your title is solid even if your video is “better” if your packaging, hook, or structure feels familiar you’re filtered out before the click
4. So what’s the fix? don’t leave the market - leave the recipe you don’t need a new niche you need a new delivery system that makes the same topic feel unfamiliar again

5. Example: “AI tools you need to try” - exploded in early 2023 - tons of creators jumped in - thumbnails became a sea of robots and ChatGPT icons audience interest didn’t die but discovery did not because the topic stopped trending but because it all blended together this is viewer fatigue when repetition dulls curiosity - and your video vanishes into the noise

6. How to break it: - Change your FORMAT Here is a prime example. Both videos are in the same niche - with the same concept - making money through YouTube shorts Person on the right innovated with a different packaging - different angle - and earned more clicks

7. Go hyper-specific - instead of “5 ways to make money” - do “how I made $1,027 selling Notion icons with 23 followers” it reactivates curiosity because it doesn’t feel like a pattern the brain already ignored
8. Shift the narrative voice - from “tips” to “experiments” - from “advice” to “autopsy” - from “generic” to “raw opinion” these small tonal shifts break the scroll they reset attention
9. Play the long game trends are fragile - formats are scalable don’t just chase what worked for others build a system that makes you hard to ignore - even in saturated spaces

10. TL;DR - no niche is too crowded - just too repetitive - sameness kills curiosity before the click - you don’t need new topics - just fresh angles - the algorithm notices novelty in delivery, not just ideas - structure isn’t optional - it’s your edge

parts: I reverse-engineered how viral YouTube scripts are written.. and here’s a blueprint you can copy for any niche 👇🧵
Before we get into it, I post a lot of YouTube related threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇
1. Start with the idea - not the topic Your video isn’t “about productivity” It’s: “The billionaire who schedules every minute of his day” - It’s specific - It’s sparks curiosity - It’s packageable

2. Map out every interesting moment before writing Take an investing video idea: - Major moments: His net worth hit $100M, SEC sued him - Minor moments: He dropped out of college, moved back home You’re not writing linearly You’re listing moments, then building a viewer experience out of them

3. Place your big moments like landmines One early - one mid - one late In a crime breakdown: - The twist can’t be at minute 2 - The confession shouldn’t come without tension Space them out Viewers will stay if they sense more payoff is coming

4. Your hook should mirror your packaging Title: “He Lost $10 Million and Laughed” Thumbnail: Sad Face + Vegas Skyline Hook: “In 2007, 20% of Caesar's Palace Casino revenue work came from one single person” - It confirms the promise - It starts the story - It keeps the curiosity alive

5. Delay the dopamine drop If you reveal the twist too soon, they’re gone Build-up = emotional context + narrative pacing In a war story: - Explain his rank, his mission, his odds of survival - Then reveal: He made it out... but his friend didn’t Without setup, there’s no payoff
6. Make the major moment unforgettable In a tech story: “He raised $200 million for an app that didn’t work” But don’t stop there The viewer now expects to leave So..👇

7. Rehook instantly after each climax Every major beat should lead to the next one “I thought that was the craziest part… until I found out what happened 6 months later" - This is retention design - You’re buying another 2 minutes with a single line Master rehooks - and your videos won’t flatline

8. Repeat the rhythm Hook - Build - Payoff - Rehook Then again That’s how you turn 4 minutes of story into 12 minutes Think of it like music: Predictable structure keeps attention even when the melody changes

9. Don’t end - hand off In a business case study: End with: “And if you thought this collapse was wild, wait until you see how the next guy made $500M doing the same thing. - End screen your previous video The algorithm loves when you design your own session chains There's nothing more powerful than signaling to YouTube that you are designing long viewer binge sessions
tldr - the viral script loop - 1 sharp idea - Plot major events - Confirm the title with your hook - Build, then drop, then rehook - Chain to the next video Work on your pacing, rhythm, and timing

parts: I studied 100+ viral videos that got 1,000,000+ views and here’s the truth: the algorithm doesn’t reward good videos it rewards viewer satisfaction - and that’s a formula you can control 👇 🧵
Before we get into it, I post a lot of AI X YouTube threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. Most creators focus on the wrong thing they chase: - clickbait - production quality - fancy edits but none of that matters if the viewer feels nothing when the video ends satisfaction = emotion + payoff the algorithm picks that up

2. Viewer satisfaction starts before the video even begins you can’t satisfy a viewer unless you’ve made a promise first → title = the promise → thumbnail = the bait → intro = the confirmation → body = the delivery no promise = no payoff = no satisfaction

3. Viewer satisfaction is impossible without demand you can’t satisfy a viewer with a video they didn’t want in the first place → reverse-engineer proven interest → monitor niche cycles → test idea demand before execution → look for high curiosity + low competition zones satisfaction starts by solving a real viewer itch

4. Packaging sets the emotional tone your title + thumbnail aren’t just about CTR - they create viewer expectations → nostalgia? then the intro better deliver memory → mystery? then you need suspense → drama? then build stakes early packaging isn’t just for clicks - it’s the viewer’s first emotional commitment

5. Your hook must escalate your promise in the first 15 seconds, you need to: - validate their click - heighten curiosity - introduce stakes open a loop they want closed this is where most creators lose viewers you need to earn the next 60 seconds

6. Then comes the over-delivery bad videos end where the viewer expected great videos go beyond: → context they didn’t know they needed → unexpected reveals → emotion layered on information → payoff bigger than the setup surprise = satisfaction

7. Emotional payoff creates the algorithmic reward when viewers feel anything - nostalgia, anger, joy, awe - they react → they comment → they rewatch → they share the algorithm sees this - and multiplies your reach

8. You can engineer viewer satisfaction every time with this formula: - start with proven demand - package to trigger memory or curiosity - confirm the promise in the intro - escalate + overdeliver - close with emotion or revelation satisfied viewers do the distribution for you
tl;dr YouTube doesn’t reward content it rewards satisfaction it rewards how the viewer feels when the video ends the algorithm listens to the viewer - make them feel something worth staying for

parts: I used AI to study how the algorithm reacts when you pivot formats too often.. And here’s why it slowly kills your reach👇🧵
Before we get into it, I post a lot of YouTube related threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇

1. The algorithm builds a "channel fingerprint" behind the scenes your upload history trains an internal model - a numeric profile of your content’s style, pacing, topic, and audience behavior this fingerprint decides: → where your videos land → who they get shown to → how confidently the system can push them

2. Every format change resets part of that fingerprint → post a story video? new pacing + new viewer behavior → post a tutorial next? now you attract different users → post a listicle after that? different watch pattern again the algorithm loses signal - and your reach weakens

3. The system doesn’t promote variety - it promotes consistency youtube doesn’t ask “is this video good?” it asks “who would want 10 more like this?” if your content is hard to model or group, it’s hard to scale creators don’t get buried because they’re bad they get buried because they’re unclassifiable

4. The algorithm relies on consistency to know where you belong YouTube groups your channel with others that have similar topics, pacing, and structure - this is how it knows who to recommend you to but when you constantly switch formats (e.g. story → tutorial → listicle), your channel keeps landing in different “neighborhoods.” → the algorithm loses confidence → you stop getting shown next to the right videos → your reach drops, even if the content is good

5. Every new format invites the wrong test audience if your format change attracts a viewer who doesn’t binge - you get penalized session drop = reach drop and now the algorithm thinks your new upload performs worse than it actually does

6. Success on YouTube is about repeatability not in content but in outcome the algorithm isn’t looking for variety it’s looking for predictable behavior you don’t have to repeat yourself you just have to make the system feel like you did

✅ how to pivot formats (without killing your channel): - test inside the old format first → change 1 variable (style, pacing, structure) per video, not all at once - bridge with hybrid uploads → combine old tone + new structure or topic to ease the algorithm (and audience) into the change - update thumbnails & titles last → keep your packaging language consistent while shifting content type beneath it - retrain your fingerprint → commit to the new format for 5–10 uploads before judging results. the algorithm needs time to re-learn your identity

tl;dr changing formats too often kills your reach because the system can’t learn who you are confused channels don’t grow clear ones do pivot slowly, signal clearly - and the algorithm will move with you, not against you

parts: I studied the top viral documentary channels on YouTube.. and here’s the system they use to blow up without crazy topics 👇🧵
Before we get into it, I post a lot of YouTube related threads Bookmark to come back and re-read this thread in the future 👇
1. Most creators think virality = better storytelling but top channels aren’t chasing stories they’re building vehicles to deliver them same story – different delivery – different result
2. The format is a funnel – hook: 0–30s – grip: 30s–2min – main story - climax - fallout – loop: CTA ending to boost next vid this is what the top documentaries repeat
3. Each phase has a job – hook: stop the scroll – grip: sell the video – meat: deliver payoff – climax: spike emotion – fallout: let it land – loop: continue the session miss one – lose the viewer

4. Great documentaries aren’t just stories they’re engineered for retention – tension resets – pacing spikes – curiosity chains they don’t just unfold – they escalate (I posted a more detailed thread on scriptwriting)

5. B-roll and voiceover are NOT the story a lot of people thing the highest quality editing wins this is not a netflix competition editing/voice overs are simply delivery tools keep it simple – the VO keeps things emotionally coherent – the visuals re-engage attention every 5–10s – the edit is the unspoken narrator it’s a silent persuasion system

6. Most beginners try to write a video pros map it first with every interesting moment listed out example: take an investing video idea: - major moments: His net worth hit $100M, SEC sued him - minor moments: He dropped out of college, moved back home you’re not writing linearly you’re listing moments, then building a viewer experience out of them
7. viral channels don’t create videos they create formats that are: – repeatable – scalable because stories come and go – but systems can scale
tldr: – don’t “write” videos – reverse engineer them – structure is a funnel, not a freestyle – your job isn’t to tell a story – your job is to keep attention until the story tells itself

author: Richard_YTS
parts: We analyzed 62 Billion+ views from 2025 to find out what makes a video go viral on YouTube. Title length, thumbnail colors, niches, video duration, we cover everything. Here’s what we found👇🧵

1. How long should you make your videos? More than 50% of the videos we studied were shorter than 15 minutes. BUT shorter ≠ better. In fact, longer videos (1 hour+) tend to perform better on average. And for videos under an hour, the sweet spot is 15–25 minutes.

Why is this? Longer videos = more watch time = stronger recommendations. But on an audience level, we’re seeing 2 things happening: 1. More watch-time coming from TVs (where longer content thrives). 2. More short-form content being consumed (which competes with short long-form content) 15-25 minutes hits the sweet spot. It’s more in-depth than shorts, is suitable for TV viewers, but still feels like an easily digestible piece of content and low time commitment. 30-60 minutes, however, is more in the danger zone. The time commitment feels long, but the watch time can’t compete with videos longer than 1 hour.

And things get even more interesting when we break video length down by niche… Below you can see the duration times that lead to most views per niche: - Gaming, Entertainment, Sports → Peak around 15–30 minutes Long enough for immersion, short enough to binge. - Finance, Business, Tech → Stronger performance at 25–40 minutes Depth + trust beat quick takes. - Movies / TV, Music, Art → Clear spikes around 20–30 minutes Context, breakdowns, and payoff matter. - DIY / Engineering → One of the strongest cases for long-form (30–45 min) Viewers want the entire process, not highlights. - Lifestyle / Vlogs → Wide variance, but 15–25 minutes consistently wins Too short lacks story, too long loses pacing. - Tech → 28mins peak also makes sense for Tech due to longer tech reviews and more in-depth explanations of product features Big takeaway: There is no universal “best” video length. But across almost every niche, 👉 mid-to-long form dominates median performance.

2. How long should your titles be? Shorter titles consistently perform best… And this makes sense because every additional word adds friction. Long titles: - Increase cognitive load. - Slow decision-making. - Feel less confident. But things get more interesting when we break down title length by characters 👇

Titles around 30 characters get nearly 60% more views than titles 70+ characters. But what’s interesting here is that we see a sharp drop off around the 60-70 character mark. This is right around where Youtube begins to cut titles off in certain displays.

But when we split this by Educational vs Entertainment content, a big difference appears… Title length matters far more for entertainment videos than it does for educational ones. This is because educational content is watched with intent, e.g. “I want to learn X” So as long as the title clearly signals the topic, extra words don’t hurt performance much. Entertainment content is clicked on impulse. The title has to: - Create curiosity - Trigger emotion - Win attention *instantly* Every extra word adds friction. That’s why we see a sharp drop-off in performance as entertainment titles get longer, while educational titles are far more forgiving.

3. Do faces help thumbnails? Overall, there’s minimal difference in performance… But when we zoom in, the impact of showing your face in a thumbnail varies greatly by niche. E.g. in the finance niche: Showing a face in the thumbnail performs 36% better on average. (Faces add trust and credibility in this niche) V.s gaming, where showing a face in the thumbnail performs 3% worse on average. (Gameplay, characters, and action frames outperform creator faces because the content is the star, not the person)

Interestingly, multiple faces consistently outperform a single face. This is likely because multiple faces imply interaction, collaboration and are generally an indication of a higher production video. Two (or more) faces instantly signal: - A moment is happening - A reaction or conflict exists - Other people found this interesting - (Maybe) a collaboration That social + emotional context stops the scroll and gets clicks.
4. Should you include text in your thumbnails? 84% of videos in our report included text in the thumbnails. But actually, thumbnails with text get 19% fewer views on average.

Why? Thumbnails without text are more inclined to visually “show” the video, adding action or conflict as opposed to just labelling. This visual cue can be picked up faster, making it easier to click. But adding text also: - Competes with the title - Slows human processing - Clutters the image

But it’s not always possible to show no text in a thumbnail. So when you do use text, whats the best approach? According to the data, thumbnails where the text is fewer than 10 characters and takes up less than 7% of the image perform best.

6. Which thumbnail colors perform best? Top-performing dominant colors: - Cyan - Green - Yellow / Orange These colors win because they: - Pop against YouTube’s mostly neutral feed - Signal energy and clarity without visual fatigue - Preserve contrast even after YouTube compression But it’s worth noting, some of these colors could be influenced due to niche patterns. E.g. sports could be affecting green, altering what it typically would be, etc.

7. How do numbers in titles impact performance? 35% of videos include numbers in their titles. But, videos with numbers get ~11% fewer views on average. Numbers often signal: - lists - explainers - tutorials Viewers click more for emotion, not structure.

8. What emotion should your titles target? We categorized the videos into 9 segments, based on their titles. And we found that the top-performing emotional buckets were: Humor Anger Controversy These emotions demand a reaction. Your title’s job isn’t just to explain the video… It’s to create emotional imbalance that clicking resolves.

9. Do negative or positive titles perform better? 66% of the videos in our data-set were neutral. But the data shows that negative titles generally perform better on average regardless of whether the content is educational or entertainment.

10. Finally, which niche should I pick? We mapped niches on two axes: Y-axis = Median Views (baseline audience) X-axis = Outlier Score (breakout potential) Top-left: big audience, low breakout Bottom-right: breakout potential, small audience Top-right: best of both worlds E.g. Gaming has: - massive median views - lowest outlier scores Why? Extreme saturation + format sameness. Top-right niches: Movies/TV, Music, and “Other” (animals, politics, history) These combine: - strong baseline demand - frequent external trends - higher outlier potential Politics → daily news Movies/TV → constant releases Music → nonstop drops Animals/history → infinite scenarios Trends manufacture breakout videos. Business & finance reality: - Low median views. Low outliers. - Saturated topics + little novelty. The niche isn’t bad, it’s just harder. Across all niches: - Median views range ~20K–70K - Outlier scores range ~1.4×–2.4× There are noticeable differences in each niche, but it's not an "end all be "all, by any means.
