parts: Everyone says YouTube growth is about: - posting more - better editing - consistency After interviewing 80+ creators over the last 2 years, responsible for billions of views, I realized: Those things barely matter. Here's what actually does (thread)...

1) The biggest growth lever on YouTube is ideas. Not editing. Not cameras. Not posting frequency. A strong idea carries: - the title - the thumbnail - the story - the retention Weak idea → nothing saves it.

2) Top creators rarely invent ideas. They observe patterns. Then apply something called: Join + Twist Step 1: Find something that works. Step 2: Change the angle. Example: Trend → Muscle suit prank Twist → “24 Hours in the World’s Most Realistic Fat Suit.” Same format. Completely new curiosity.

3) Great creators constantly study what already works. They ask: • What videos keep showing up? • Why did this one get millions? • What’s the hook? Then they create a version with their own angle. Creativity on YouTube isn’t randomness. It’s pattern recognition.
4) Most creators design thumbnails wrong. They try to make them: • cinematic • aesthetic • detailed But YouTube thumbnails have one job: Be understood in 0.5 seconds. Simple always beats pretty.

5) Your brain reads thumbnails like a story. Usually left → right. So strong thumbnails guide your eye through the narrative. Example structure: Before → Arrow → After That’s why transformation thumbnails dominate YouTube.

6) Another pattern top creators use: Formats. Formats are repeatable video structures. One good format can produce dozens of videos. Examples: • Visiting expensive gyms • Testing extreme diets • Investigating trends Formats build momentum.
7) Great creators treat ideas like a database. They constantly write them down. Even bad ideas. Why? Because ideas evolve. A random thought today might become a viral video later.

8) Advanced creators organize content into buckets. Example fitness channel buckets: • diet experiments • food challenges • gym experiences • investigations Then they combine ideas from those buckets. Almost like building with Lego.
9) One mistake almost every beginner makes: Posting videos people only watch if they already know you. Example: “My back workout routine.” Why would a stranger click that? They won’t.

10) Early YouTube strategy should be mass appeal. Your video should work even if someone: • has never heard of you • doesn’t follow your niche • doesn’t know your story Once people care about you… Then you earn the right to make personal content.
11) Another important reality: Even the best creators don’t go viral every upload. Research shows: Top creators average 3 breakout videos out of 10. Meaning 70% of videos are just learning.
12) Instead of chasing viral hits… Smart creators focus on eliminating bad ideas. Because if you remove weak videos: Your average views increase automatically. This is called loss mitigation.

13) Fast-growing channels also find gaps. Not bigger audiences. But specific problems. Example: Instead of “self improvement” Focus on something specific like: “Recovering from narcissistic relationships.” Specific audience Specific pain Explosive growth.
14) And finally… The biggest retention killer on YouTube: Long intros. Creators spend 1–2 minutes explaining the video. But viewers already clicked. Give them value immediately.

parts: We’ve helped 100+ YouTubers blow up their channel. And from our experience, 80% of what causes a channel to blow up is the ideas! So here’s the 13 step ideation checklist we follow that pretty much guarantees viral videos👇

1. Feasible - Can you realistically make this video well? Even if you have the best idea in the world, if you can’t execute the actual content well (whether it be budget, time, resources or any other reason), then it’s not a good idea for your channel at this time. But save it - maybe in the future you’ll be able to make it. (Alongside each of these points in the checklist, we’ll also be showing real client results from working with the 1of10 team to prove that this ideation method actually works!)

2. Positive Data - Is there evidence that this idea would perform well? What videos can you find on YouTube (or potentially outside of YouTube) to suggest that there’s a high interest in this idea. (The video in this graph was inspired from outside the niche, and it absolutely crushed for the creator becoming one of their most viewed videos of all time)

3. Negative Data - Is there recent evidence that this idea isn’t working well? Just like how you should look for positive data, it’s also important to look for reasons not to make an idea. Are there recent videos on similar topics that underperformed despite having good content? (We’ve been working with this creator for roughly 1 year, and in that time the views have increased by 50%, despite reducing output!)

4. Unique - Can you do it first, escalate, twist or improve on what’s out there? It’s never good to directly copy on YouTube, so ideally your idea is unique in some way. This can be through taking inspiration from outside your niche, twisting ideas, improving on what’s already out there etc. We’ll be doing a full breakdown on all the ways you can do this soon!

5. Title - Can this idea be clearly described in 10 words or less? While not every title needs to be fewer than 10 words, if an idea takes more than 10 words to explain, it’s usually too complicated and oftentimes not a good idea. Of course, as with everything on this list, there are exceptions!

6. Thumbnail - Can you visually build curiosity around this idea in a thumbnail? This is really important, and often something even experienced creators leave til too late. But having a clear idea of 2-3 thumbnail variations you can test for each video before filming is a cheat code for choosing the best ideas. If you can’t package the video well, then it’s not a good idea for YouTube.

7. Content - Is there enough interesting content behind this idea? This is trap many creators fall into, but they’ll have an idea that sounds great on paper, but when it comes to actually filming the idea, the content itself is boring or just doesn’t work. Always think through what the actual content behind an idea would look like in this stage.

8. Hook - Can you actually create an intriguing hook for this video? This is a niche one, but can you actually write a hook for this video that delivers on the packaging and sets up the rest of the video without ruining the payoff?

9. Goals - Does this video fit the longterm goals of your channel? This one is super important. Just because a video can get a lot of views doesn’t necessarily mean you should make it. Does this video bring the right audience and take your channel closer to where you want it to be in 5 years time? A viral video with the wrong audience can do more harm than good!

10. TAM - Is there a large enough audience for this idea? This is a simple one, but it’s super important to check that there’s actually a large enough TAM for your idea to meet your goals. A quick way to assess this is to find the highest viewed videos covering the same topic / similar topics and assume that is roughly the maximum TAM for your content.

11. Audience - Does this video appeal to you core audience, casual viewers and new viewers? If your goal is to grow, it’s important to make sure that every video appeals to your regular viewers, but also a new viewer seeing your channel for the first time could also watch and enjoy the content.

12. Risk - Are there any audience, reputation, timing or relevance concerns? This is typically not an issue, but a good thing to check just in case. Could there be any potential backlash from you making this idea that you’re not comfortable with?

13. Seasonality - Is this the best time to post this video? Is this the best time to post this video, or would it perform better if you posted it at some other point in the future? Or maybe this idea would have crushed 2 months ago, but now it’s not a good time to make.

parts: I’ve worked on videos totalling billions of views across hundreds of channels. And the one thing every viral video has in common? A great idea. So here’s the exact frame work I use to find banger ideas (in ANY niche)👇

Before we go deeper, it’s important to understand that every viral idea can be broken down into 2 core components (and technically a 3rd as well, but more on that later). The Interest Topic This is essentially what the video is about. This will depend on what your audience is actually interested in. In the weapons niche this could be ‘Katana’. In the the fitness niche, this could be ‘burning fat’ Each interest topic will have a different Total Addressable Market (TAM), but also a different level of vitality, which is based on the TAM, supply of content already out there, and it’s relevance right now. While interest topics can fluctuate over time, especially due to over-saturation or external factors, they’re generally consistent and often times you can use older data to support this.

The idea format The format is essentially the framing of the interest topic / the structure of the video. ‘$1 vs $1,000,000’ - which is essentially showing contrast between 2 extremes. ‘Coldest vs Hottest’ or ‘Biggest vs Smallest’ would essentially be the same format. ‘Give Me 9 Minutes, and I’ll show you how to ____’ - an example from the education niche. The format dictates the structure of the video and framing of the topic. It’s usually less of an indicator of TAM, but can be heavily affected by the supply of other videos (i.e. if a lot of videos have been done in a certain format, then it may lose it’s novelty over time), and so relevance is super important here.

To have the best chance of coming up with a viral idea, we want to find data-backing for BOTH the interest topic and core format of the idea. This will give us a strong indication of whether an idea will perform well. The key here is to not take inspiration all from one place, but to mix and match different pieces of data and combine them into one unique idea that has support from several different data points. To do this, there are 5 main ways we can find inspiration for these, and you should be looking in all of these places.

1. Inside your own channel This is going to be the strongest indication for which interest topics and formats work well, and which ones don’t. After all, this is data from your exact audience. A great example of this is what we did with one of our clients, Mike Shake. 2 years ago, we made a idea where Mike tested ‘How Dangerous is a Whip?’ At the time, this video crushed and was one of his most viewed videos. So 1 year later, we created another video around the same interest topic, Whips, but this time Mike built a crazy dangerous whip. The result? 14 Million views.

2. Inside your niche One of the easiest ways to find winning ideas is by looking at what’s already overperforming inside your niche. Here you’re looking for formats and interest topics. In fitness, for example, supplements and performance enhancers is an interest topic that consistently produces huge outliers and had a huge TAM. This led us to this outlier for Will Tennyson, ‘I Tried EVERY Legal Performance Enhancer’. But we actually found the format for this idea from the next step which is…

3. Inside Adjacent Niches Adjacent niches are essentially niches that share either a large audience overlap, topic overlap, or audience characteristics overlap. A good way to find adjacent niches is to think of your niche as a topic on a family tree. Let’s use day trading as an example. You want to find the ‘parent’ topic for your niche, which in this case could be money / finance. Then, you want to find the other topics under that main parent niche. Essentially finding the sibling topics for your niche. In this case, that could be topics like ‘investing’ or ‘crypto’ etc.

Adjacent niches are generally best for finding formats. You can sometimes get an idea for interest topics here, but often times these would be different due to the fact that the niches and topics covered are completely different. Here’s an example we helped to ideate for Jdub, taking inspiration for the format from the Youtube education niche, and adapted it into the trading niche.

4. Broader YouTube Searching broader YouTube can be a great way to find fresh formats that haven’t been brought into your niche yet. But here it’s even more important than in any of the previous steps to really understand exactly why a format or idea worked so well, in order to find out whether that might translate into your niche or what you need to adapt. We recently did this in the fitness / weight loss niche, by taking inspiration from an investing video. ‘The [Something] Secret to [Desired Outcome]’

5. External But YouTube isn’t the only place you can find inspiration for ideas. You can also look outside of YouTube to find both interest topics and formats. For example, you could find which topics have a super high interest on Reddit, TikTok, Instagram or even Google search prediction. You could also pull popular formats used on TV shows and bring those over to YouTube. And this can apply to thumbnails as well. Here’s an example of an idea and thumbnail I came up with for Ohara, where I was actually inspired from a Google search recommendation and a scene in Naruto.

But the real key here is to understand the psychology behind why each of these formats or interest topics performed so well in the first place in order to find out how you can adapt them without losing the core substance that made them perform so well in the first place. For example, taking the $1 vs $1,000,000 framing as an example. Why did this format work so well? Humans love contrast, and this takes it to the extreme. It shows the absolute cheapest vs most expensive element in a given interest topic. ‘Money’ and ‘Expensive’ things are a super high universal intrigue point across YouTube and content in general. Retention optimised structure. The structure of this idea leads to the biggest payoff (the $1,000,000 item) at the end of the video. So viewers have to watch til the end to see the highest interest point.

But there’s also a third thing to look out for, and this is viral vectors. Viral vectors (or ‘viral vextors’) are essentially things that are of high interest across different niches. For example, ‘Japanese’ or ‘Invisible’. These are not restricted to one particular niche, and are used to supplement an interest topic and make it extra enticing. They don’t always fit in every idea, but can be used to take a good idea, and make it amazing.

parts: Here’s how 4 thumbnail/title changes saved this video stuck at 35k views to then explode to 300k views with CTR literally doubling. Thought this was cool to share! /thread
1) Initially started with a Midjourney generated thumbnail. That failed right off the bat and was a 10/10.

parts: What is the best niche on YouTube? We used an LLM to analyze over 300,000 videos to find out (bookmark this) 👇

Here’s how to read it: Y-axis = Median Views Higher Y = bigger audience + higher baseline view potential. So if a niche sits higher on the chart, it gets more views on average. X-axis = Outlier Score This tells you how often a video overperforms the channel’s norm. Example: If your median is 30k views, and one video gets 90k → that’s a 3× outlier. Outliers = growth. No outliers = no breakout = slow channel. So ideally, your niche sits in the top-right quadrant: High median views + high outlier potential = easier growth + more upside. Let's break down the results for some popular niches...
Gaming has massive median views… …but the lowest outlier score. Why? It’s the most saturated niche on YouTube. Everyone is doing it → harder to break out. Same story for broad entertainment.

Compare that to Movies/TV, Music, and the category labeled Other (animals, politics, history). These niches have: - High outlier scores - Strong median views - Constant new trends - Unlimited content supply They’re built for momentum. Think about it...

Politics → daily news cycle Movies/TV → new releases every week Music → nonstop drops & discourse Animals/history → endless hypotheticals and scenarios Trend-focused niches = more opportunities for viral spikes. Health & fitness shows the same pattern but with lower median views. Why lower? Because it’s fundamentally educational, and education generally gets fewer views than entertainment. But the outlier score is still solid because trends still drive the niche. Meanwhile, finance/business is the opposite of what most people expect...

People think “teaching money = tons of views.” But the data shows: Low median views + low outliers. Why? It’s saturated… and not much new happens. Everyone’s been talking about the same side hustles and business models for years. BUT here's an important reminder...

Even though niches do differ… The full range of median views spans roughly 20k → 70k. The outlier range spans 1.4 → 2.4. These are not life-changing gaps. Your unique angle, experience, or skill matters way more than the niche itself. A lower Y-axis (view potential) on the "business" niche doesn't matter if you're running a really successful company, you'll be able to easily out-perform the average :) Or, a low X-axis (outlier score) on the "food" niche doesn't matter if you take somehow advantage of trends as a chef :) So, if you have special skills, experience, etc, pick the niche that aligns best with that! But if you don’t have a standout skill or story yet? If you’re going faceless? If you want the highest statistical advantage...

parts: 🚨 Brutally honest truths about YouTube Automation NOBODY talks about (bookmark for later) If you're doing faceless YouTube in 2025, this thread is going to save you months of pain 🧵

1) Stop overthinking your niche. Here are the criteria for finding niches: - At least 300K views/month - Started < 90 days ago - Possibility to hit 1M views/month and/or $5K+/month - More views than subs = even better That's it. Stop being a perfectionist.

2) Multi-language = multi-income. A channel in English is cool. But that same video dubbed in Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese? You're now building an empire. (Almost) the same effort, but 5x output Don't sleep on this ;)
3) You're supposed to copy, but copy smart. Replicating a format that works is how you win. But don't just CTRL+C everything blindly. Match the structure and then add your own twist/unique angle.

4) Most people fail because they stop showing up. Not because their videos suck. Not because the niche is "saturated" They just… quit. This game rewards consistency more than anything else. If you just keep uploading and improving, you will win. Eventually.

5) AVP (Average % viewed) is overrated. AVD (watch time in minutes) is 👑 A 15% AVP on a 60-minute video = 9 mins watch time A 50% AVP on a 6-minute video = 3 mins watch time What is YouTube's goal? To keep people on the platform as long as possible. So which video is YouTube more likely to recommend?

6) Your thumbnail is your thumbnail. Read that again. If no one clicks, no one watches. And if no one watches, it doesn't matter how good your content is. Thumbnails are not optional. They're 50% of the game... so important!
7) You're not too late, you're too slow! There are hundreds of faceless channels blowing up right now with easy content. Not because they're early. But because they TAKE ACTION.
8) Your team will only scale if your systems do. Don't blame your editor if the videos suck. Blame your systems. Good SOPs = good output. Structure everything (Loom videos, guides, documents, etc.)!
9) Diversify your channels Relying on one channel is risky. Diversify your content across multiple channels and niches. Don't put all your 🥚🥚🥚 in one basket

10) YouTube Automation is NOT free Everyone is selling the dream: "Start a YouTube channel with $0 using AI" And it sounds great... until you try it Because even a basic setup costs you at least $50/month... - ChatGPT Plus for scripts - ElevenLabs for voice overs - Canva Pro for thumbnails That's your entry ticket. And if you're serious, like actually trying to build a brand or scale multiple channels you'll spend closer to $300-$500/month just on tools/software. It's doable for a lot of people, but it isn't free.

11) Some think 10-15 videos will tell them if a channel "works". That's false (for most channels). For AI channels, you need 30-50 videos minimum before you can even judge if it's getting picked up by the algo. So don't give up after two weeks. Most people quit right before things start working...

12) RPM is everything (yet so overlooked) Most creators focus only on views. But the real game is RPM (revenue per 1,000 views). $5 RPM vs $75 RPM is the difference between: - $3,000/month - and $45,000/month You can literally 15x your income WITHOUT more views...

13) Long videos = more money. 8-minute videos = mid-roll ads = higher RPM 120-minute videos = even more mid-roll ads = even better RPM YouTube makes more money → so they pay you more. It's that simple ;)

14) You WILL fail at your first niche. Don't expect your first channel to take off. It (probably) won't. Most people: ❌ Fail first niche ❌ Fail second niche ✅ LEARN and win with the third, fourth or fifth niche.. But the thing is... if you never give up, you CAN NOT fail!

15) Political/news channels are risky AF. Yes, they can go viral. Yes, they can make you $50K+/month. But… If your channel gets banned, YouTube does't pay out. Even if you earned $50K And you might get in trouble with your AdSense..

16) You need SOPs SOPs are genuinely your secret weapon. If your team keeps messing up, it's (usually) not their fault, it's your system that just isn't good enough. Good SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) make your business scalable (also important if you want to sell a channel). No/bad SOPs = chaos as soon as you try to scale. So make good SOPs. Create Loom videos, detailed explanations, guides, FAQs, etc.

17) This is a business, not a side hustle. If you want YouTube to replace your job, then you need to treat it like a job. Start with 1-2 hours/day to learn the basics. Then go full-time. 8+ hours/day. This is how people scale to $30K, $70K, even $100K+/month.

18) Low barrier = heavier competition The game is (getting) crowded, but that's not an excuse. YouTube Automation has a low barrier to entry. Anyone with $50 and WiFi can start. That means competition is (getting) high(er). But most people upload bad quality videos, give up too early, or just don't know what they're doing. But if you're willing to upload to quality content, and be consistent/patient, you'll most likely win.

parts: Most people making $100K+/month on YouTube have one thing in common that nobody talks about: They're all using a YouTube CMS. And if you're serious about YouTube, you NEED to understand this Here's everything you need to know about a CMS (bookmark this) 👇🏼🧵

So first, what even is a YouTube CMS? CMS = Content Management System It's basically a special dashboard YouTube gives out to people who manage a ton of content. Like if you have 40, 50, 100 channels and you need to manage them all in one place instead of logging in and out like a maniac.

But here's the thing YouTube doesn't just hand these out to anyone. You need to be a "large content holder" Meaning you either run a massive network of channels, or you own a huge library of copyrighted content (like music, stock footage, etc) It's not something regular creators get access to, in fact it's almost impossible to get one yourself (but more on that later)

Now there are 2 types of CMS and this is where it gets interesting: 1. Managed CMS (also called O&O - Owned & Operated) 2. Affiliate CMS (also called MCN) And the difference between these two is huge.. Let me explain both:

Managed CMS (O&O): This is where you CREATE channels directly inside the CMS from scratch They're 'owned and operated' (O&O) by the network These channels are basically born with a silver spoon.. they get special treatment from YouTube straight away

Affiliate CMS (MCN): This is where you LINK existing monetized channels to a network. So your channel is already running and you connect it to get extra benefits. This is how most YouTubers work with networks actually (since they don't create a new channel of course)

Now why does this matter for faceless channels? Because a Managed CMS gives you insane advantages: > Highest trust score on YouTube > Algorithm boost from day 1 > 99% monetization acceptance rate > Enhanced protection from demonetization waves (who doesn't need that right now haha) > Your videos get pushed harder It's literally unfair lol

And the trust score thing is huge.. I've literally seen channels upload their first video ever (with zero subscribers, brand new).. And get 3,500 views in 8 hours. And, nowadays, that just doesn't happen with regular channels. You'd be lucky to get 50 views lol So the CMS basically tells YouTube "hey this content is legit / more trusted" and boom, instant push

Another crazy benefit is Content ID.. So basically if someone steals your content anywhere on YouTube, you can claim the revenue from their video For example, people steal my ASMR content constantly But I registered it with Content ID so every time someone rips it, I get paid Adds an extra 5 figures per month btw ;)

And then there's the protection side. This is probably the most important part honestly. Since for channels that are STARTED inside a managed CMS, I've seen ZERO cases of inauthentic content demonetizations on AI storytelling. Like actually zero But for channels that are linked later, I've seen some get hit So, again, there's a huge difference in a Managed CMS and an Affiliate CMS

So if you're doing AI storytelling channels, sleep content, or anything that's kinda in the grey area, a managed CMS is basically your insurance policy YouTube has to manually review your content to take it down (and that almost never happens) Versus regular channels that get auto flagged all the time..

And you can also do stuff like: > Block specific countries (especially useful if you have a bad audience but want to sell something for example) > Get a verified badge whenever you want > Track who's using your content across YouTube > Access live chat support with ACTUAL humans Stuff regular creators can't do.

But, here's the problem Getting your own CMS is basically impossible for most people. You need: > Massive content catalog > Multiple high performing channels > Hit quarterly revenue thresholds > Get partner manager approval > Apply through official YouTube forms And even then most applications get rejected

Also CMSs are worth insane amounts of money Like stupid amounts And you can't just 'buy' one. You have to legally acquire the entire company that owns it Lawyers, contracts, informing Google with 30 day notice, the whole thing I know because I literally just did this

I recently acquired my own CMS (@FGMnetwork) Not partnered with one, but actually own the thing 100% outright This has been my dream for 10+ years, since I first started on YouTube as a kid To finally achieve this goal is really insane honestly ❤️

And now it's growing extremely fast The results we're seeing are actually crazy.. people are getting views from day 1, monetization is happening fast and channels protected Really proud of what we're building with it & how many people it's helping This is the stuff I dreamed about back when I was 15, first coming across YouTube networks.. back then it was Freedom MCN and I used to have a subnetwork called "DutchNetwork", this was my first side hustle.

But, let's get back to the valuable info.. And this is an important warning: There are some CMSs out there offering 'instant monetization' without the 1K sub / 4K watch hour requirements Stay away from those right now! WMG and others are under heavy scrutiny from Google for selling access If they get shut down, you get zero money. So it's NOT worth the risk

But what are your actual options? 1. Build massive channels and try to get your own CMS (good luck honestly) 2. Work with an existing CMS that accepts partners (@FGMNetwork) 3. Purchase a YouTube CMS by acquiring an entire company which takes 100s of thousands of dollars + months of work Option 2 is how 99% of creators actually get access Including most of the people crushing it right now

And for context Every single person I know making serious money on YouTube is using a CMS. Like everyone. Because once you hit a certain scale, you need that extra layer of protection It's not optional if you want to go past $100K, $200K+ per month.

parts: I've created over 100 YouTube channels in my career. Most of them failed. But the ones that succeeded have made me over €5,000,000+. Here are the 10 biggest mistakes people make with YouTube automation (that I learned the hard way):

1. Testing too few niches Most people try one niche, it fails, and they quit. When a channel blows up, it's often because I tried 8-10 similar channels with different angles. You need quantity to find what works. I upload 8-10 new channels per week now.

2. Giving up too soon I see this all the time - people launch a channel, post 5-10 videos, get no views, and quit. You haven't even given YouTube enough data to understand your content. Don't judge a niche until you've posted at least 33 videos consistently.

3. Ignoring recent niche success patterns One of my best strategies: Find channels that have blown up in the last 3 months (not 3 years). Look for channels with less than 100 days since start that are getting insane views. This is how we found the retro niche which is 80-90% dominated by our students now.

4. Getting video length completely wrong Short videos = lower RPM. One of my soap ASMR channels made over $800,000 by focusing on 20+ minute videos. For sleep content, I make 8-hour videos that get $35-50 RPM. One 6,000-view video can make $300 while only costing $30 to produce.

5. Not understanding copyright properly At 16, I got sued by Fox TV for Family Guy content. At 18, all my channels were terminated. That was my turning point. I switched to properly licensed content. You either transform content completely or get proper permissions. There's a reason I've generated over €5M since that shift.

6. Focusing on viral trends instead of evergreen niches Trends fade. Evergreen niches like finance, health, and personal development stay relevant for years. I'd rather have a channel making $5K/month for 5 years than $20K for 2 months.

7. Missing the mult-ilanguage opportunity This is HUGE and almost nobody does it. Every channel I start now launches in 8 languages simultaneously. The original video costs $35-40, but each additional language only costs about $5 more. I only need 1 language to succeed to pay for all eight.

8. Hiring the wrong team I had pretty bad team members at first. Nothing was running systematically well. Now I have 35+ people across multiple offices in Bali, Hanoi, and online. Start with one solid VA, then slowly build systems before expanding. One manager now oversees 6-8 people.

9. Not optimizing for maximum RPM People don't realize certain niches have 5-10X higher RPM than others. When I was uploading Family Guy illegally, I was getting an RPM of $85. Crime storytelling channels can get $20+ RPM on 2-hour videos. This directly affects your profitability - choose niches with high RPM potential.
10. Making inconsistent thumbnails Most channels use random thumbnail styles across their videos. The most successful channels have a clear, consistent template.

YouTube automation is HARD. It takes time, effort, and constant testing. But with 19 years in the game, I can tell you it's still one of the most profitable online businesses when done right. Success doesn't happen overnight. It took me 14 days to hit $1,000/day with my record channel, but most take months. It's not about luck. It's about systems, persistence, and learning from failure.

Top 5 Deep Dive · For each top 5 competitor: what they do well, their signature format, their top outlier title, and the one thing driving their growth. D. INPUT Channel URL (used to identify the niche): [CHANNEL URL] STEPS - Run channel_resolver and get_niche_overview to lock the niche. - Run find_outlier_faceless_channels filtered to the niche, under 50K subs, high outlier scores. Hook Template · The dominant hook type with a fill-in-the-blank opener - 3-4 sentences of actual voiceover, not a description. C. Structure Blueprint · The 5-7 section skeleton every video should follow, with what happens in each section. D. Pacing Rules · When to go dense, when to breathe, where to place the biggest payoff. E. Evidence Mix · Which types of evidence to lean on, with ratios (e.g. 40% data, 30% story, 30% expert). F. Exit Formula · How every video should end. G. 3 Things Never To Do · Based on what's missing from the winners.

A theme appearing 3+ times across the 5 videos is real signal, not an outlier. OUTPUT A. Content Demand List · Top 10 specific video ideas viewers explicitly asked for. For each: what they asked, how many times, proposed title. B. Unanswered Questions · Top 5 questions the existing videos didn't answer but viewers keep asking. Each becomes a standalone video with a proposed title. C. Disagreement Angles · 3 debates in the comments worth making a response video about. D. Story Hooks · 3 real viewer stories from the comments that could open a future video. Quoted, with context. E. Next 3 Videos · The 3 highest-leverage ideas from A/B/C/D, ranked for production priority.

Log niche, avg views, sub count, comment-to-view ratio. - Run youtube_channel_outliers. Take top 5 videos. - Run youtube_video_comments on all 5, top-sorted, 100 per video. 500 comments total. - Read every comment. G. 3 Hook Ideas · Three 3-4 sentence hooks written for this persona. Each activates a different trigger.

Log subs, avg views, views-to-subs ratio, 90d growth, upload frequency, top geography, RPM estimate. - Run youtube_channel_videos for the last 90 days. Split into top 20% by views and bottom 20%. Run get_batch_channel_metrics on all. parts: 🚨 Harsh truths about YouTube Automation NOBODY tells you: If you're building a faceless YouTube channel and want real results, this thread is for you! 🧵

1) YouTube Automation is NOT free Everyone is selling the dream: "Start a YouTube channel with $0 using AI" And it sounds great... until you try it Because even a basic setup costs you at least $50/month... - ChatGPT Plus for scripts - ElevenLabs for voice overs - Canva Pro for thumbnails That's your entry ticket. And if you're serious, like actually trying to build a brand or scale multiple channels you'll spend closer to $300-$500/month just on tools/software. It's doable for a lot of people, but it isn't free.

2) Some think 10-15 videos will tell them if a channel "works". That's false (for most channels). For AI channels, you need 30-50 videos minimum before you can even judge if it's getting picked up by the algo. So don't give up after two weeks. Most people quit right before things start working...

3) RPM is everything (yet so overlooked) Most creators focus only on views. But the real game is RPM (revenue per 1,000 views). $5 RPM vs $75 RPM is the difference between: - $3,000/month - and $45,000/month You can literally 15x your income WITHOUT more views...

4) Long videos = more money. 8-minute videos = mid-roll ads = higher RPM 120-minute videos = even more mid-roll ads = even better RPM YouTube makes more money → so they pay you more. It's that simple ;)

5) You WILL fail at your first niche. Don't expect your first channel to take off. It (probably) won't. Most people: ❌ Fail first niche ❌ Fail second niche ✅ LEARN and win with the third, fourth or fifth niche.. But the thing is... if you never give up, you CAN NOT fail!

6) Political/news channels are risky AF. Yes, they can go viral. Yes, they can make you $50K+/month. But… If your channel gets banned, YouTube does't pay out. Even if you earned $50K And you might get in trouble with your AdSense..

7) You need SOPs SOPs are genuinely your secret weapon. If your team keeps messing up, it's (usually) not their fault, it's your system that just isn't good enough. Good SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) make your business scalable (also important if you want to sell a channel). No/bad SOPs = chaos as soon as you try to scale. So make good SOPs. Create Loom videos, detailed explanations, guides, FAQs, etc.

8) This is a business, not a side hustle. If you want YouTube to replace your job, then you need to treat it like a job. Start with 1-2 hours/day to learn the basics. Then go full-time. 8+ hours/day. This is how people scale to $30K, $70K, even $100K+/month.

9) Low barrier = heavier competition The game is (getting) crowded, but that's not an excuse. YouTube Automation has a low barrier to entry. Anyone with $50 and WiFi can start. That means competition is (getting) high(er). But most people upload bad quality videos, give up too early, or just don't know what they're doing. But if you're willing to upload to quality content, and be consistent/patient, you'll most likely win.

4) Now the fun part... animating the image For this, you'll have 2 options. I will explain both clearly The first option is Kling AI 1. Go to "Image to Video" 2. Paste this prompt: "Cinematic video. Static camera. The character moves slowly in dramatic slow motion, with subtle, expressive body movement." 3. Click "DeepSeek" to improve the prompt 4. Click "Use prompts" 5. Set duration of the video (5/10 seconds) 6. Click "Generate" It even adds sound (if you turn this on). Out of everything I’ve tested, Kling AI gives the best motion video quality.

5) The seconds option: Higgsfield AI This is great for basic camera motion like: - Dolly in/out - Pan left/right - Zoom in/out - Tilt - Etc, etc You can also use the prompt I shared above for this AI.

6) You can use both depending on the shot In my opinion... Kling AI = better for movement/character animation & sound. Higgsfield AI = better for smooth, minimal camera motion. (this video below was made using Higgsfield AI)

7) That's it You can literally go from a sentence like "guy walking into a jail cell" to a fully animated scene using just AI tools And it's pretty cheap ;) Remember to use this specific GPT: bit.ly/45Scukk

parts: How to come up with BANGER video ideas 📈 Let's break down the entire YouTube ideation process (bookmark) 🧵👇🏼

STEP 1: OUTLIER RESEARCH (Foundation) Use a tool like @1of10media or do it manually. Set filters: - 3X+ multiplier - 100K+ views - Channels under ~500K subs You're hunting for high signal outliers, aka videos that BLEW UP! Manual method: search, open, compare views to channel average, look for 3X+

STEP 2: VALIDATE TAM (Total Addressable Market) This is where most people f*ck up. Go to YouTube, type your keyword, sort by view count. If you see multiple videos on your topic with around ~500K+ views, that's good news! This means there's actual demand for your topic. A lot of people pick topics where there's no demand at all. This way, you know there IS demand. And it gets even better if your competition has low-quality videos!

STEP 3: COMPETITION ANALYSIS (The 4-Tier Matrix) Here's a matrix on competition analysis: Direct → same niche, same style Indirect → same niche, different format Adjacent → different niche, same audience (goldmine) Distant → different niche, same attention market (advanced)

STEP 4: VALIDATION CHECKLIST Before you commit, ask yourself this: - Can you actually make it? - Would strangers click? - Will 80% of your subs care? - Could it go viral? - Does it fit your brand? - Is the title/thumbnail packageable?

STEP 5: AVOID SHITTY OUTLIERS Not every viral video is a good one to copy. Here's what to avoid: - Wrong audience (like a gaming outlier on a finance channel) - Unfair advantage (collabs you can't do) - Built on momentum - Dead topics (only ONE video ever worked on it... and that was luck)

STEP 6: FORMAT TRANSFER TECHNIQUE Find a viral format outside your niche → adapt it For example: "I Read 100 Productivity Books So You Don't Have To" turn it into... "I Watched 100 Business Movies So You Don't Have To"

parts: 🚨 Scriptwriting is the most overlooked skill in faceless YouTube. Here's how to write scripts that keep people watching (bookmark for later) 🧵

1) The most important thing to understand about faceless YouTube is that your words ARE your personality. With faceless YouTube channels, there is no face to connect with So your script is the channel's identity. Every line must serve two jobs: - Keep attention - Deliver value/entertainment If your script can't do that, it doesn't matter how "aesthetic" your visuals are. They'll click away. And it all starts with this next part 👉🏼

2) Most people write faceless scripts like they're writing blog posts. This is the first mistake. People don't read YouTube videos. They listen (and watch). So your script must sound good out loud, not just look good on paper. Here's how to fix that: - Short sentences - Conversational tone - Clear transitions - No jargon (unless explained) You want the viewer to feel like the video is talking to THEM directly, even if it's an AI-generated voice-over.

3) The most critical part of your script is the first 30 seconds. The hook. If your script loses them in the intro, no edit can save it. The hook must do three things: - Validate the click (did the video deliver what the title promised?) - Create an open loop (a curiosity gap that needs to be closed) - Set the tone and expectations Bad hook: "In this video, we're going to talk about habits." Better hook: "Most people think discipline is about waking up at 5AM. What actually matters is something nobody talks about, and it's probably why your life still feels stuck." That's how you buy another 30 seconds of attention, because now the viewer wants to know what the thing is that no one is talking about...

4) After the hook, most beginner faceless scripts fall into the same trap: trying to say too much, and too fast Instead, build your script around 3 to 5 strong payoffs A payoff is any moment that delivers meaningful value / insight. That is basically the reason people keep watching. So don't clutter your video with 8 different ideas in 6 minutes. Go deep on fewer points and use transitions to carry momentum. Use lines like: - "But here's where it gets really interesting" - "Most people stop here, but what happens next is insane" - "This next part might sound obvious, but almost no one actually does it" Keep creating open loops. That's how you hold 60%+ retention

5) The best faceless scripts follow a tension-and-release rhythm You create tension by introducing a problem, a mistake, or a contradiction. You release it by offering a solution, explanation, or unexpected twist. Bad scripting gives away the answer too fast. Great scripting lets the viewer "earn" it Here's an example pattern you can steal: - Problem: "Most people fail to save money because they think budgeting is about cutting back." - Tension: "But they're completely wrong, and this one mindset shift proves it." - Release: "Instead of focusing on expenses, start XYZ. Because XYZ." That is how you teach AND entertain!

parts: YouTube live streaming is one of the most UNDERRATED strategies right now You can be "live" 24/7, without actually being live... Let me explain the full setup, why it works, and why it pays way more than regular uploads (bookmark this): 🧵

What live streaming actually is (in the context of faceless YouTube): first of all, you're NOT going live in the traditional way but instead, you're uploading a long-form pre-edited video (could be 60-90 min for example), and streaming that on a loop (using an external platform) you schedule the stream to run for exactly 11 hours, 55 minutes NOT over 12 hours, because YouTube only saves livestreams that are under 12 hours to your channel afterward so every stream becomes two assets: - a stream that gets priority in the algorithm while it's live - a long-form video saved to your channel, and YouTube will still keep recommending it to people, even after the livestream has ended and you can automate this loop indefinitely

Tools you can use: → Upstream: simple, clean UI, around $30/month for 1 stream at a time But there are also some other tools like Restream, Streamlabs, OneStream, etc: all let you loop pre-recorded content as "live" you just upload your video(s), paste your stream key from YouTube, choose start and end times, and schedule it from that moment on, the tool handles everything your PC can be off. you don't need OBS. you don't even need to log in again haha

But why does this work (and why it makes more money): livestreams get a "ranking boost" when they're live YouTube literally gives "Live Now" content more visibility in homepage and suggested placements but there's more: → people fall asleep with them on → they let them play in the background for hours → they often watch it on TVs So with all that, it means your watch time, session duration, and retention all go up, which pushes your stream even more which means you'll also get higher RPMs: from my testing, RPMs on livestreams (especially in sleep/TV ambient niches) are often 30-50% higher than regular uploads a few reasons why: → more ads shown over longer sessions → like I said, a lot of people watch on TVs which means a higher RPM → the AVD is insanely long

So here's why it's PERFECT: 1) you don't need daily uploads 2) you don't need dozens of videos 3) you don't even need to be awake lol you can take a few high-quality pieces of content, loop them into a single long video, schedule it once, and let it run indefinitely big faceless channels like Dr. Insanity are starting to notice it as well, they're live streaming now

But how can you apply this? 1. Create a long-form video (60-120 mins) or compile multiple clips into one file 2. Upload the video to Upstream or a similar tool 3. Set your stream time: 11:55:00 (so it gets saved after) 4. Get your stream key + RTMP URL from YouTube Studio 5. Set your title to something that has "LIVE" / "24/7" in it 6. Schedule the stream 7. Make bank
